passage: In the canteen queue, Tanvir spotted Damini at a far table, staring at her tray with the corners of her mouth turned down. His first thought was that she was sad, or that something had gone wrong with her placement interview. He almost turned away to give her space, but instead he carried his tea over and sat down. "Hey, you look a bit low. Everything okay?" Damini looked up and laughed. "Oh, it's my face! My mouth just sits like this when I'm thinking. I was working out whether to have the rice or the pasta." She thought, then added, "Though I am a bit tired after last night's study." Tanvir smiled. "Good to know. Both things, then."

qa.q: Where was Damini sitting?
qa.a: She was sitting at a far table in the canteen.

qa.q: What did Tanvir think Damini's downturned mouth meant, and what was the truth?
qa.a: He thought she might be sad about her placement interview, but Damini said it was just her thinking face, with some tiredness too.

qa.q: Why was walking over better than turning away?
qa.a: A resting face can look sad without being sad, so asking told Tanvir the real situation while offering company.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt about Tanvir's question?
qa.a: She probably felt cared for and amused that her face had worried him.

grounding: A young adult notices a friend's downturned mouth corners, thinks she may be sad or tired, and asks instead of assuming.

"You look really sad," Sumit said, dropping his bag by the sofa.
Urmila glanced up from her laptop. "Do I?"
"Your mouth is all turned down. Did something happen?"
"I don't think so." She thought for a second. "Actually, it might be the deadline. I've been at this proposal since morning and my brain feels like porridge. So tired, maybe a bit stressed, but not sad."
"Okay. I wasn't sure, so I asked."
"Thanks. Most days my face just does that, though. Ask me anyway."
"Deal." Sumit put the kettle on. "Tea, and then I'll read your proposal with fresh eyes?"
"Yes, please." Her mouth finally turned up.

qa.a: He put his bag by the sofa.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Sumit said she looked sad?
qa.a: She was tired and a little stressed about the deadline, but not sad, though she admits her face often looks like that anyway.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that helped Urmila?
qa.a: He asked instead of assuming, then offered tea and a fresh pair of eyes on her proposal.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Urmila said she wasn't sad?

passage:
In my first year at college in Ludhiana, I thought my friend Gurpreet was sad all the time.
Her mouth turned down at the corners, even in class, even at the canteen. I'd whisper, "You okay?" and she'd say, "Yes, why?" I thought she was hiding something.
One day, after two weeks of this, I asked properly, away from everyone. "Gurpreet, you always look a bit down. Are you really okay? Or tired? I don't want to assume."
She burst out laughing. "Shreya! That's just my face. My whole family has it. My father looks like he's at a funeral when he's watching cricket and his team is winning."
I laughed too, but I felt a bit silly. I'd built a whole story about her secret sadness from the shape of her mouth.
Now I know: a resting face isn't a mood. When I want to know how someone is, I ask.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's father look like when watching cricket?
qa.a: He looks like he's at a funeral, even when his team is winning.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling after learning it was Gurpreet's resting face?
qa.a: Shreya felt a little silly and relieved, realising a whole story about secret sadness had been built from the shape of a mouth.

qa.q: What did Shreya learn about reading faces?
qa.a: That a resting face can look sad without being sad, so asking is better than assuming.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet see the repeated "You okay?" questions?
qa.a: Gurpreet was probably puzzled by them, since she wasn't sad at all.

grounding: The account shows a young adult reading a friend's downturned mouth as sadness and asking, discovering it was a resting face.

passage:
Supervisor's note - Rekha, research lab, Thursday
For the past week, our new intern Pranav has had downturned mouth corners and a flat expression most of the day. Two lab members asked me if he was unhappy with the project or with us.
I didn't want to assume. On Wednesday I asked him to help me carry samples to the cold room and said, "You've looked a bit low this week. How are you doing?"
He laughed, tiredly. "Sorry, Ma'am. I'm not sad. I've been studying for my entrance exam till two every night. I'm exhausted. And honestly, my face always looks like this."
I thanked him for telling me. I shifted his tasks so he wasn't handling delicate samples late in the day, and suggested he leave on time this week.
I also reminded the team: a tired or resting face isn't always sadness. Asking helped.

qa.q: Until what time has Pranav been studying?
qa.a: Till two every night.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling during that week?
qa.a: Pranav felt exhausted from late-night study, not sad, though his resting face made him look low.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that was helpful?
qa.a: She asked privately instead of assuming, then adjusted his tasks and encouraged him to leave on time.

qa.q: How did the two lab members read Pranav's face?
qa.a: They read his downturned mouth as unhappiness with the project or the team.

grounding: The supervisor's note shows a downturned mouth being read as sadness when it reflected tiredness and a resting face, and asking clarifying it.

passage:
Sunday
Ayesha's mouth has been turned down all week. At first I thought, that's just her face; last month she told me people always think she's sad. So I left it.
But today at the hostel mess she barely touched her food, and her eyes were puffy too. Resting face doesn't make your eyes puffy.
I didn't want to assume either way. After dinner I sat on the steps with her. "I know your face sometimes looks sad when you're not. But this week, are you actually okay?"
She was quiet. Then: "My grandmother is in hospital back home. I didn't want to make a fuss."
I'm glad I asked. If I'd decided it was just her face, I'd have missed it.
We went for a walk, and she called her mother while I sat with her.
Asking works both ways. Sometimes it's nothing. Sometimes it's something.
- Devika

qa.q: What else did Devika notice besides Ayesha's mouth?
qa.a: Her eyes were puffy too, and she barely touched her food.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling that week?
qa.a: Ayesha felt sad and worried about her grandmother in hospital, but didn't want to make a fuss.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Devika to ask instead of assuming?
qa.a: Ayesha's resting face can look sad without being sad, so only asking could show whether this time it was real sadness.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had decided it was just Ayesha's face?
qa.a: Devika would have missed Ayesha's real sadness about the grandmother, and Ayesha would have carried the worry alone.

grounding: The diary shows a young adult noticing a friend's downturned mouth and asking instead of assuming, discovering real sadness this time.
